citations.quote:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let
$W=(W_1,\ldots,W_k)$, for a finite $k\ge1$, be a random element of the product
measurable space $\mathcal W=\prod_{j=1}^k\mathcal W_j$
([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]],
[[def-measurable-space]]). The law of $W$ is the pushforward probability
measure defined in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. Let
$\mathcal R$ be a nonempty finite set of observation patterns with its
discrete sigma-algebra, and let $R:\Omega\to\mathcal R$ be a random element.

For each $r\in\mathcal R$, specify the recorded coordinate set
$I_r\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and its complement
$J_r=\{1,\ldots,k\}\setminus I_r$. The **observed projection**
$W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r)$ is the coordinate projection into
$\mathcal W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r):=\prod_{j\in I_r}\mathcal W_j$, and the
**missing projection** $W_{\mathrm{mis}}(r)$ is the projection into
$\mathcal W_{\mathrm{mis}}(r):=\prod_{j\in J_r}\mathcal W_j$. An empty
coordinate tuple takes values in a one-point measurable space. The **observed
record** is $O=(R,W_{\mathrm{obs}}(R))$ in the disjoint union
$\bigsqcup_{r\in\mathcal R}(\{r\}\times\mathcal W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r))$,
where a set in the disjoint-union sigma-algebra is measurable exactly when
each pattern section is measurable. The pattern records which coordinates are
available; it does not replace an unrecorded full-data value by zero.

Fix the full-data/observed-data partition of
[[def-full-observed-and-missing-data]]. A **response mechanism** is a
specified conditional law $g(r\mid w)$ of the pattern $R$ given full data
$W=w$, represented by a probability kernel from the full-data space to the
finite pattern space
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]],
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]). In a parameterized model, write
the response kernel as $g_\psi$; it must be a probability distribution over
patterns for each full-data value.

Relative to a specified full-data law, the mechanism is **missing completely
at random (MCAR)** when, for every pattern $r$, $g(r\mid w)$ is constant in
$w$ almost surely. It is **missing at random (MAR)** when, for every pattern
$r$, there is a measurable function $h_r$ on that pattern's observed-data
space such that
$$g(r\mid w)=h_r(W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r))\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
For a family of full-data laws, the condition is required under each law with
the same response mechanism and observed-coordinate function. It is
**missing not at random (MNAR)** when MAR fails for at least one pattern, for
the declared full-data and observed-data partition. MCAR is a special case of
MAR, since a constant is a function of the observed coordinates.

These conditions concern a supplied version of the conditional law; values
off the full-data model's support do not affect the classification. This
definition does not assert that a response mechanism is empirically true or
that every joint law comes with a selected conditional kernel.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Assume AC. If $\mu$ and $\nu$ are sigma-finite positive measures on the same
measurable space and $\nu\ll\mu$, then the Radon–Nikodym class
$d\nu/d\mu$ has a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative. Every
finite-valued representative of that class is nonnegative
$\mu$-almost everywhere.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim:
By [F3] and [F4], choose a countable cover $E_n$ of $\mathcal W$ with
$\mu(E_n)<\infty$, replace it by the increasing cover
$F_n=\bigcup_{j\le n}E_j$, and put $A_1=F_1$ and
$A_n=F_n\setminus F_{n-1}$ for $n\ge2$. The $A_n$ partition $\mathcal W$ and
each has finite $\mu$-measure. Set
$c_n=2^{-n}/(1+\mu(A_n))$ and define
$\rho(E)=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\mu(E\cap A_n)$. Rearrangement of nonnegative double
series shows that $\rho$ is countably additive; moreover
$\rho(\mathcal W)\le\sum_n2^{-n}<\infty$, and $\rho(E)=0$ exactly when
$\mu(E)=0$, since every $c_n>0$ and the $A_n$ partition $\mathcal W$. Thus
$\rho$ is finite and equivalent to $\mu$.

For every pattern $r$, the coordinate projection $\pi_r$ is measurable by
[F1], so $\kappa_r=\rho\circ\pi_r^{-1}$ is a finite measure. If
$\kappa_r(B)=0$, equivalence gives $\mu(\pi_r^{-1}B)=0$, and [F3] gives
$P_\theta(\pi_r^{-1}B)=0$. Thus the full-data marginal
$B\mapsto P_\theta(\pi_r^{-1}B)$ is absolutely continuous with respect to
$\kappa_r$. The pattern sublaw
$B\mapsto\int_{\pi_r^{-1}B}g_\psi(r\mid w)\,P_\theta(dw)$ is bounded above by
that marginal because the kernel section lies in $[0,1]$, so it too is
absolutely continuous. By [A1, F6, F8], choose finite-valued nonnegative
densities $q_{\theta,r}$ and $\ell_{\theta,\psi,r}$ for these finite measures.

For a measurable set $A$ in the observed disjoint union, its pattern
sections $A_r=\{x:(r,x)\in A\}$ satisfy
$P_{\theta,\psi}(O\in A)=\sum_r\int_{A_r}\ell_{\theta,\psi,r}\,d\kappa_r
=\int_A\ell_{\theta,\psi}(r,x)\,d\lambda_O$. These densities therefore
represent the observed-record law relative to the stated $\lambda_O$; their
total mass is one because
$\sum_rP_{\theta,\psi}(R=r)=\int\sum_rg_\psi(r\mid w)\,P_\theta(dw)=1$.
The full-data marginal densities $q_{\theta,r}$ likewise integrate to one.

In the product-reference case, for each pattern $r$ and
observed-coordinate measurable set $B$, the product decomposition in the
Statement gives the pattern sublaw as
$\int_{B\times\mathcal W_{\mathrm{mis}}(r)}
p_\theta(x,z)g_\psi(r\mid x,z)\,
d(\nu_r^{\mathrm{obs}}\times\nu_r^{\mathrm{mis}})$. Its integrand is
nonnegative and product-measurable, so [F9] gives the displayed
missing-coordinate integral as a density relative to
$\nu_r^{\mathrm{obs}}$. Applying the same argument with $g$ omitted gives
the displayed marginal density $\bar q_{\theta,r}$. Empty blocks use the
one-point unit measure as stated.

Step 1.1 permits a zero response probability, in which case the nonnegative observed-pattern density is zero.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

derivations.claim: For any $P\in\Theta_{a,b}$, write $c=P(R=0,Y=1)$. Since $P(R=0)=1-a$, one has $0\le c\le1-a$, and $m(P)=P(Y=1,R=1)+P(Y=1,R=0)=b+c$. Hence $b\le m(P)\le b+1-a$.

Conversely, fix any $m\in[b,b+1-a]$ and assign $P(Y=1,R=1)=b$, $P(Y=0,R=1)=a-b$, $P(Y=1,R=0)=m-b$, and $P(Y=0,R=0)=1-a-m+b$. Each entry is nonnegative by the bounds on $a,b,m$; the four entries sum to one. This law has response rate $a$, observed success mass $b$, and mean $m$, so every point of the interval is attained, including both endpoints.

Under each such law, the pushforward law of $O$ has masses $b$ at $(1,1)$, $a-b$ at $(1,0)$, and $1-a$ at $(0,0)$, independent of $m$. Thus all parameters in $\Theta_{a,b}$ are observationally equivalent. If $a<1$, the interval has positive length $1-a$, so it contains distinct means and the estimand is not identifiable. If $a=1$, it is the singleton $\{b\}$ and the mean is identified as $b$.

For each $P\in\Theta_{a,b}$ use the finite conditional response kernel in [F8]. Under MAR, the probability $g_P(0\mid Y)$ depends only on the empty observed projection for pattern $R=0$, so it is constant $P_Y$-almost surely. Hence $g_P(1\mid Y)=1-g_P(0\mid Y)$ is also constant $P_Y$-almost surely; its constant is $P(R=1)=a$, by integrating over $P_Y$. Therefore $b=P(R=1,Y=1)=aP(Y=1)$, and for $a>0$ the mean is $b/a$. If $a=0$, every law in the interval construction of step 1.2 has $R=0$ almost surely; its selected kernel is constant on the support of $Y$, so it is MCAR and hence MAR. The whole interval $[0,1]$ therefore remains compatible with MAR.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement imposes 0≤b≤a≤1, and step 1.2 constructs a probability law for every m in the resulting nonempty interval.
Step 3.1 treats a=0 directly: b=0, the compatible interval is [0,1], and no division by a is made.
Step 2.1 treats a=1: the interval collapses to {b}, so all data are observed and the mean is identified.
Steps 1.2 and 2.1 include a=1, where the missing mass is zero and the interval is a singleton.
Step 1.2 verifies nonnegativity and attainability at m=b and m=b+1-a, where an unobserved-outcome cell may be zero.
Step 1.2 gives the four joint masses explicitly; no family of representatives or witnesses is selected.

citations.quote:
Assume AC. Let $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_k)$ have a full-data model dominated by a
common sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ on the finite product measurable
space $\mathcal W=\prod_{j=1}^k\mathcal W_j$, with selected finite-valued
density representatives $p_\theta$ as in
[[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]] and [[def-likelihood-density]]. Let
$\mathcal R$ be a nonempty finite pattern set, let $I_r$ and $J_r$ be the
observed and missing coordinate sets for pattern $r$, and write
$\pi_r(w)=W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r)$ for its measurable coordinate projection. Let
$g_\psi(r\mid w)$ be a supplied response probability kernel as in
[[def-mcar-mar-and-mnar]], and define the joint model by
$$P_{\theta,\psi}(dw,\{r\})=g_\psi(r\mid w)P_\theta(dw).$$

Fix a finite positive measure $\rho$ equivalent to $\mu$; such a measure
exists for every sigma-finite $\mu$. For each pattern put
$$\kappa_r(B)=\rho(\pi_r^{-1}(B))$$
for measurable $B\subseteq\mathcal W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r)$, and define the finite
measure on the observed disjoint union by
$$\lambda_O(A)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\kappa_r(\{x:(r,x)\in A\}).$$
The full-data marginal law of $W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r)$ and the pattern-$r$
observed sublaw $B\mapsto P_{\theta,\psi}(R=r,\pi_r(W)\in B)$ are absolutely
continuous with respect to $\kappa_r$. Choose finite-valued nonnegative
Radon--Nikodym density representatives $q_{\theta,r}$ and
$\ell_{\theta,\psi,r}$ for these measures. Then the observed record
$O=(R,W_{\mathrm{obs}}(R))$ is dominated by $\lambda_O$ and has density
$\ell_{\theta,\psi}(r,x)=\ell_{\theta,\psi,r}(x)$ at $(r,x)$.

In the product-reference special case where
$\mu=\nu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^k\nu_j$, each $\nu_j$ is sigma-finite, and the
coordinate reordering $w=(x,z)=(W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r),W_{\mathrm{mis}}(r))$
identifies $\nu$ with
$\nu_r^{\mathrm{obs}}\times\nu_r^{\mathrm{mis}}$, where
$\nu_r^{\mathrm{obs}}=\bigotimes_{j\in I_r}\nu_j$ and
$\nu_r^{\mathrm{mis}}=\bigotimes_{j\in J_r}\nu_j$, one may instead use the
pattern reference $\nu_r^{\mathrm{obs}}$, with disjoint-union reference
$\lambda_O^{\mathrm{prod}}(A)=\sum_r\nu_r^{\mathrm{obs}}(\{x:(r,x)\in A\})$.

An empty coordinate block is a one-point space with unit mass.

$W=w$, represented by a probability kernel from the full-data space to the
finite pattern space
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]],

Relative to a specified full-data law, the mechanism is **missing completely
at random (MCAR)** when, for every pattern $r$, $g(r\mid w)$ is constant in
$w$ almost surely. It is **missing at random (MAR)** when, for every pattern
$r$, there is a measurable function $h_r$ on that pattern's observed-data
space such that
$$g(r\mid w)=h_r(W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r))\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

the same response mechanism and observed-coordinate function. It is
**missing not at random (MNAR)** when MAR fails for at least one pattern, for
the declared full-data and observed-data partition. MCAR is a special case of

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f : X \to [0,+\infty]$ be measurable. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ define

$$s_k := \sum_{j=0}^{k2^k-1} j2^{-k}\, \mathbf{1}_{\{j2^{-k} \le f < (j+1)2^{-k}\}} + k\,\mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge k\}}.$$

Then each $s_k$ is a simple measurable function,

$$0 \le s_k \le s_{k+1} \le f,$$

and $s_k(x) \to f(x)$ for every $x \in X$. If $E \subseteq X$ is a set on which
$f \le M < +\infty$, then $s_k \to f$ uniformly on $E$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a finite complex measure with $\nu\ll\mu$. If $h$ is a representative of $d\nu/d\mu$, then
$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
More generally, if
$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$
In particular, whenever the Lebesgue integral of $gh$ is defined, one has
$$\int g\,d\nu=\int gh\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim:
For each MAR factor in the Statement, replace any measurable
almost-sure version $h_{\psi,r}$ by
$h^*_{\psi,r}=\min(1,\max(0,h_{\psi,r}))$. Since every kernel evaluation
$g_\psi(r\mid w)$ lies in $[0,1]$ and equals
$h_{\psi,r}(\pi_r(w))$ $P_\theta$-almost surely for every $\theta$, clipping
leaves each of those identities true and makes $h^*_{\psi,r}$ pointwise
$[0,1]$-valued.

For a measurable observed-coordinate set $B$, put
$u=\mathbf1_Bh^*_{\psi,r}$. By [F4], the integral of any nonnegative simple
function of $\pi_r(W)$ under $P_\theta$ equals its integral under the
pushforward law $Q_{\theta,r}$; [F5] supplies increasing simple
approximations to $u$, and [F6] passes to their limit. Since
$Q_{\theta,r}$ has density $q_{\theta,r}$ with respect to $m_r$, [F7] gives
the same integral as $\int_Bh^*_{\psi,r}(x)q_{\theta,r}(x)\,dm_r(x)$,
again by simple approximation and monotone convergence. MAR therefore yields
$P_{\theta,\psi}(R=r,\pi_r(W)\in B)
=\int_Bh^*_{\psi,r}(x)q_{\theta,r}(x)\,dm_r(x)$.
Thus $h^*_{\psi,r}q_{\theta,r}$ is a selected density version for the
observed pattern section; in the product-reference case this agrees as a
density class with the coordinate integral in the Statement.

Because $q_{\theta,r}(x)\ge0$ and the same nonempty parameter set $\Psi$
is allowed for every $\theta$, the profile satisfies
$\sup_{\psi\in\Psi}\ell_{\theta,\psi}(r,x)
=q_{\theta,r}(x)\sup_{\psi\in\Psi}h^*_{\psi,r}(x)$. The multiplier is finite
and common to every $\theta$, and if it is zero the record has zero likelihood
for all $\theta$. For fixed $\psi$, whenever $h^*_{\psi,r}(x)>0$ and
$q_{\theta_2,r}(x)>0$, the ratio at $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ is
$q_{\theta_1,r}(x)/q_{\theta_2,r}(x)$. A target depending on $\psi$ can still
depend on the response factor, and a non-Cartesian allowed parameter set need
not permit common profiling.

Let $Y,R\in\{0,1\}$, with $R=1$ meaning that $Y$ is observed, and encode the
observed record as $O=(R,RY)$. When $R=0$, the zero in the second recorded
coordinate is a placeholder and does not assign the missing full-data value
$Y=0$. Put
$$a=P(R=1),\qquad b=P(R=1,Y=1),\qquad 0\le b\le a\le1.$$
Let $\Theta_{a,b}$ be the set of all joint laws $P$ of $(Y,R)$ with these
values of $a$ and $b$, and let the statistical model map $P\in\Theta_{a,b}$
to the law of $O$. For each individual $P$, use its finite conditional
response kernel specified below when assessing the MAR clause; arbitrary
null-state values do not affect that classification. The full-data mean $m(P)=P(Y=1)$ is an estimand on this
model. Its set of values over $\Theta_{a,b}$ is exactly
$$[b,b+1-a].$$
Consequently, without a MAR restriction, the mean is not identifiable when
$a<1$; it is identified as $b$ when $a=1$. If MAR also holds, then for $a>0$
the mean is $b/a$, while for $a=0$ it remains unidentified.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: For the first model, $g(1\mid x,y)=1/2$ is constant in $(x,y)$, hence MCAR by [F2]. In the second, both pattern probabilities are functions of $x$ alone, which is recorded for both patterns, so MAR holds by [F3]; it is not MCAR because the probability differs at $x=0$ and $x=1$. In the third, $P(Y=0\mid X=x)=P(Y=1\mid X=x)=1/2$ for each $x$, and $g(0\mid x,0)=3/4$ while $g(0\mid x,1)=1/4$. Thus the pattern-$0$ probability cannot be a function of its observed coordinate $x$ alone, so the mechanism is MNAR by [F4].

Each row of the table contains nonnegative entries summing to one. Under either law, $P(R=1,Y=1)=1/4$, $P(R=1,Y=0)=1/4$, and $P(R=0)=1/2$, so the observed record laws agree and have $a=1/2$, $b=1/4$. The means are $1/4$ and $3/4$. For the selected finite kernels in [F6], $P^{-}$ has $g_{P^-}(1\mid1)=1$ and $g_{P^-}(1\mid0)=1/3$, while $P^{+}$ has $g_{P^+}(1\mid1)=1/3$ and $g_{P^+}(1\mid0)=1$. In each law the pattern-$0$ response probability also differs across the two values of $Y$, although the observed projection for that pattern is empty; hence neither law is MAR. This agrees with [F5] and shows the observed respondent mean $1/2$ does not identify the population mean.
